41.0.0.en: 1 “Listen unto me, O islands; and let the tribes renew their strength: let them come near; then let them speak: let us come near together to judgment. 2 Who raised up from the east him whom victory meets at his feet? He gave the nations before him, and made him rule over kings: he gave them as the dust to his sword, and as driven stubble to his bow. 3 He pursued them, and passed safely; even by the way that he had not gone with his feet. 4 Who hath wrought and done it, calling the generations from the beginning? I the LORD, the first, and with the last; I am he.” 5 The isles saw it, and feared; the ends of the earth were afraid, drew near, and came. 6 They helped every one his neighbour; and every one said to his brother, “Be of good courage.” 7 So the carpenter encouraged the goldsmith, and he that smootheth with the hammer him that smote the anvil, saying of the soldering, “It is good”: and he fastened it with nails, that it should not be moved.

41.0.1.en: The prophet Isaiah presents a wonderful poetic picture of the victory that Israel gains through Cyrus, who allows them to return from captivity.

41.0.2.en: The prophet affirms that what will happen by means of Cyrus is not of his own accord but by divine ordering.

41.0.3.en: “Listen unto me, O islands; and let the tribes renew their strength: let them come near (let them keep silent); then let them speak: let us come near together to judgment” [1]. He addresses the distant islands, which the waters surround on every side. This is an allusion to Israel in captivity in Babylon, far from his country, surrounded by the waters of trials to drown him... He asks him to listen first, then to be silent, and then to speak and converse with God, as in a trial between two equals or two parties.

41.0.4.en: Listening and silence do not mean passivity, but mean lifting the heart to God and meditating on His wonderful works, awaiting His continual salvation of His people and His Church. Silent prayer moves heaven itself; God hears it and answers it, as happened with Moses crying out in his heart (Ex 14:15) and with Hannah in the Temple (1 Sam 1:13).

41.0.5.en: * Let us now come to the silent prayer of Hannah, the mother of Samuel, how it was a delight before God: it opened the barren womb and removed her reproach, for she bore a Nazirite and a priest.

41.0.6.en: Father Aphrahat * Jonah prayed a prayer without a voice (Jn 2); the shepherd was silent in the belly of the fish, and from within the dumb creature his prayer crept upward and God heard it in the heights, for his silence was a cry.

41.0.7.en: Mar Ephrem the Syrian * If your mouth is quietly silent, your heart is always aflame with the warmth of the Spirit!

41.0.8.en: If you speak with your tongue while your heart is not moved to prayer, your speech is a loss!

41.0.9.en: Silence your tongue so that your heart may speak... and silence your heart so that God may speak!

41.0.10.en: The Spiritual Elder * Stillness makes you shine like the sun and purifies you from ignorance.

41.0.11.en: * If you want to know a man of God, tell it from the constancy of his stillness.

41.0.12.en: Mar Isaac the Syrian * Those who stand in the presence of Christ, who pour all their attention into divine things and are freed from all the distractions of the world, keep always the hidden prayer of the heart and the spiritual thoughts of the mind, rejecting every temporal thought that darkens the soul and driving it away, so that it does not distract them from thinking about God...

41.0.13.en: * Would that we, beloved, put off the burden of temporal care and spend all our time in thoughts of God; by this our soul is purified and soars in the heavenly realms toward God. For the divine words remove the rust from the mind and take away from it the weight of temporal things, and lift it to the vision of divinity...

41.0.14.en: * Let us pray in a hidden way with humility of heart, without any desire to be puffed up in pride concerning the outward show of prayer, which makes us lose the reward.

41.0.15.en: Father Martyrius Silence must be accompanied by the inner dialogue of love between God and the soul. At the beginning of this book God asks us to enter with Him into a dialogue so that we may seize the forgiveness of our sins (Isa 1:18), but here He wants us to draw near to Him and speak with Him closely through the language of stillness; we hear Him with our inner ears and converse with Him with our tongue of the heart, and our spiritual insight is opened so that we may perceive closely the saving mysteries of God... This is what He meant by His saying, “Let them come near; then let them speak” [1].

41.0.16.en: Father Martyrius says: [Let us imitate Mary, the sister of Lazarus, who sat at our Lord’s feet and heard His words (Lk 10:39; Jn 11:1); by her love her soul was lifted up to heaven at His words. For this reason our Lord gave a good testimony about her: “Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Lk 10:42). Let us imitate this blessed woman in the good part that she chose, for our Lord is even now near to us...]

41.0.17.en: What did the prophet Isaiah see and what did he hear as he drew near to God in stillness?

41.1.0.en: “Who raised up (the righteous one) from the east, him whom victory meets at his feet? He gave the nations before him, and made him rule over kings: he gave them as the dust to his sword, and as driven stubble to his bow” [2]. From the literal side he means Cyrus, whom the Lord raised up from the east, granting him victory at his feet, meaning that He gives him swiftness of movement; wherever he settled with his army, victory was achieved for him. Most scholars hold that Cyrus, the destroyer of Babylon, was known for justice, even though his army and his men were known for violence and ferocity. He became a symbol of the Lord Christ in His salvation, not from the captivity of Babylon or any other, but from the captivity of the devil and sin.

41.1.1.en: In some translations, such as the Septuagint, he is called “righteous,” and some Jewish rabbis thought that the discourse here is about Abraham, the father of the fathers, who came from the east to possess, through his seed, the land of Canaan. But the Fathers of the Church throughout the ages, such as St. Jerome, St. Cyril, Eusebius of Caesarea, Theodoret and Procopius, hold that the discourse here concerns the Messiah.

41.1.2.en: The Hebrew word for victory here is “Sedek,” which means “righteousness or divine judgment or victory, etc...” For the Lord Christ, who is without sin, the only Righteous One, came and meets us with a righteousness that is His own, to bestow it on us. His victory is not through wars and physical resistance, but through establishing us in His righteousness.

41.1.3.en: The sword of Christ and His holiness are His evangelical word, which turns evil into dust and stubble, while souls are purified from every blemish; by this He reigned over the Gentiles, shattering all evil in them.

41.2.0.en: “He pursued them, and passed safely; even by the way that he had not gone with his feet” [3], as though Cyrus had come so swiftly that he seemed not to touch the ground with his feet. This also pointed to the swift spread of the preaching of the Gospel of salvation, or the saving work of Christ.

41.3.0.en: This salvation is accomplished through God Himself, who is “the first”; He worked, and remains working in the life of His people from the beginning to the end [4].

41.3.1.en: The Lord put a question in the judgment of the peoples, and since no one answered, He answered: “Who hath wrought and done it, calling the generations from the beginning? I the LORD, the first, and with the last; I am he” [4]... It is He who called the generations from the beginning to draw near to Him and enjoy His salvation, and He remains, even with the others (the appearance of pagan gods), the same, unchanging in His love through the generations.

41.4.0.en: He called humanity from the beginning to live with Him, but it rejected the Creator and made for itself gods unable even to protect themselves, made by the carpenter and the goldsmith and the one who smooths with the hammer and the soldering... each encourages the other so that the statue may come out perfect, and the nails hold it fast “that it should not be moved” [7].

41.4.1.en: There is no basis of comparison between idols that need someone to make them and someone to guard them and someone to repair them lest they fall into ruin, and a Creator Christ who moves with practical love to renew our unstable, corrupt nature.

41.4.2.en: By exposing the falsity of the idols He declares the weakness of the nations, in order to call them to the greatness of Christ, who alone is able to save!

41.5.s.en: 2. My servant whom I have chosen:

41.5.0.en: 8 “But thou, Israel, art my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, the seed of Abraham my friend. 9 Thou whom I have taken from the ends of the earth, and called from the corners thereof, and said unto thee, Thou art my servant; I have chosen thee, and not cast thee away. 10 Fear thou not; for I am with thee: look not around; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness. 11 Behold, all they that were incensed against thee shall be ashamed and confounded: they shall be as nothing; and they that strive with thee shall perish. 12 Thou shalt seek them, and shalt not find them, even them that contended with thee: they that war against thee shall be as nothing, and as a thing of nought.”

41.5.1.en: He exposes the weakness and disorder of the nations, and declares that they are dust and stubble [2], and calls them to enter the new Israel to enjoy, through the saving work of Christ, the divine friendship that Abraham, the father of the believers, experienced, for He says:

41.5.2.en: “But thou, Israel, art my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, the seed of Abraham my friend” [8]. God chose Abraham as His friend, called him from a pagan nation that did not know God, to become righteous, raising him up from the east, with victory meeting him at his feet [2]. God has not changed; He still seeks to justify and befriend sons of His, calling them from among unbelieving people to accept faith in Him and become His beloved.

41.5.3.en: * Abraham, who was called the Friend, was found faithful, because he obeyed the words of God.

41.5.4.en: St. Clement of Rome Who is the chosen servant but the Lord Christ, who took the position of a servant to represent weak humanity, and so establishes a covenant in its name before the Father, sealing it with the precious blood. As St. Gregory of Nazianzus says: [He was called a servant to serve many in truth... He came as a servant in the flesh and by birth for the sake of our life, that He might free us, saving us from the bondage of sin.]

41.5.5.en: The incarnate Word of God became a servant so that, as we who are servants abide in Him, we may hear the divine voice calling to us:

41.5.6.en: “O Israel my servant”: you who were strangers and far off have become the new Israel, a holy Church and a justified people, good servants united with the Only-Begotten Son who became a servant.

41.5.7.en: “Jacob whom I have chosen,” as the Lord Christ said to His disciples: “Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you.”

41.5.8.en: “The seed of Abraham my friend”: you have become the sons of Abraham spiritually, his sons in faith, so you are counted beloved to Me as your father was a friend to Me.

41.6.0.en: “Whom I have taken from the ends of the earth, and from the corners thereof I called him” [9]: I brought you from the farthest parts of the inhabited world and called you from among the nations...

41.6.1.en: “Fear thou not; for I am with thee”: this is the subject of My calling, and the secret of My choosing you, and the aim of My salvation, that I may be with you...

41.7.0.en: “I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness” [10]: I will be a help and support to you, because I have justified you by My blood, so that you have become righteous in Me, worthy of every help and support against your opponents who perish, and against your adversaries whom you seek and do not find, since they have become as nothing [11, 2].

41.7.1.en: In former times you sought nails to hold the plates of gold and silver on the wooden idols so that they would not fall [7], to gain for them outward beauty and give them precious value; but now I hold your right hand so that you are not shaken, I pour My glory into you and give you My righteousness, and you are glorified: “For I the LORD thy God will hold thy right hand, saying unto thee, Fear not; I will help thee” [3].

41.7.2.en: The phrase “Fear not” is often repeated in this book... for God knows the true disease of human nature, or its dangerous germ, namely fear, which shatters our peace, our joy and our inner glory. The secret of this fear is our feeling of isolation and loneliness: no companion, no helper, no one who grasps the reality of our feelings, no one who shares the depths of our inner emotions. Therefore the Savior comes forward Himself to accompany us, not from outside but by dwelling in our depths, filling the inner emptiness, and being the companion and helper and the One who satisfies all our inner needs, who shares our hidden feelings.

41.7.3.en: In brief, what does God our Savior offer? He offers Himself to us and so gives us: being with Him, help, strength, and He lifts us up to Himself! In other words, He comes down to us so that we may receive Him into our life, and so He supports us with His grace and is our hidden helper, and carries us to Himself so that we share with Him His eternal heavenly glories.

41.8.s.en: 3. The weak worm becomes a new threshing instrument:

41.8.0.en: 13 For I the LORD thy God will hold thy right hand, saying unto thee, Fear not; I will help thee. 14 “Fear not, thou worm Jacob, thou remnant of Israel; I will help thee, saith the LORD, and thy redeemer, the Holy One of Israel. 15 Behold, I will make thee a new sharp threshing instrument having teeth: thou shalt thresh the mountains, and beat them small, and shalt make the hills as chaff. 16 Thou shalt fan them, and the wind shall carry them away, and the whirlwind shall scatter them: and thou shalt rejoice in the LORD, and shalt glory in the Holy One of Israel.”

41.8.1.en: The two words “Fear not” are repeated three times in verses [10-14]; this was necessary for poor souls shattered by despair during the captivity and the sense of humiliation and slavery. But God reassures by every means His faithful believers who agree to enter with Him into a covenant, so that they do not fear or tremble. The secret of their hope and strength is their enjoyment of Him as their King, who gives Himself to them that they may enjoy Him, saying: “For I the LORD thy God will hold thy right hand, saying unto thee, Fear not; I will help thee” [13].

41.8.2.en: Thus God ascribes Himself to them: “I the LORD thy God,” that they may take refuge in Him not as a stranger to them but as their own “God,” who longs to receive them to Himself and keep them in Him. It befits them not to be slow in seeking His help, for He holds their right hand, longing for their salvation more than they themselves long for the salvation of their souls; therefore He does not cease to say: “Fear not; I will help thee.”

41.8.3.en: It is noted that God calls Himself “I the LORD thy God.” If He called Himself “Jehovah” (Ex 3:14; 15; 6:2) when He called Moses to save the people from the bondage of Pharaoh, He made clear to him the secret of His name, which is: “I AM THAT I AM” (Ex 3:14), affirming that He is ever existing, dwelling among His people without His love or care changing. Thus God presents His name with many titles to reassure His believers, among them:

41.8.4.en: “Jehovah-jireh” (Gen 22:14), which means “the LORD is seen,” for Abraham saw with the eyes of faith the unique sacrifice of Christ, which gives the power of the Resurrection.

41.8.5.en: “Jehovah-shalom” (Judg 6:24), which means “God is peace,” for Christ, the Word of God, is our peace (Eph 2:14); by Him we enjoy reconciliation with God as the secret of our inner peace and our peace with others.

41.8.6.en: “The LORD that healeth thee” Jehovah ropheka (Ex 15:26): He longs to heal our souls and our bodies as the true Physician of humanity.

41.8.7.en: “The LORD our righteousness” Jehovah-Zidkenu (Jer 23:6); in Christ we have become righteous (1 Cor 1:30), since we bear fellowship in His nature and enjoy His righteousness in us.

41.8.8.en: “Jehovah-nissi” Jehovah- nissi (Ex 17:15) (the LORD is my banner); God has become my banner, going before my steps in the spiritual battle; He is the secret of my victory and the sign of my triumph over the enemy of good.

41.8.9.en: “Jah Jehovah” Jehovah-yah (Isa 12:2), which means “I AM THAT I AM,” “I am who I am,” as One present among His believers whose love for them does not change.

41.8.10.en: “Jehovah-shammah” Jehovah- Shammah (Ezek 48:35), that is, “the LORD is there,” which points to the declaration of the presence of the Lord in the Church of the New Testament, in the midst of the new Israel, since she has become the icon of heaven, which is “the tabernacle of God with men” (Rev 21:3).

41.9.0.en: God declares His love for His people, whom He called “the worm of Israel,” in order to raise up from it a new sharp threshing instrument able to thresh the mountains and crush them and fan them so that the storms scatter them, for He says: “Fear not, thou worm Jacob, thou remnant of Israel; I will help thee, saith the LORD, and thy redeemer, the Holy One of Israel. Behold, I will make thee a new sharp threshing instrument having teeth: thou shalt thresh the mountains, and beat them small, and shalt make the hills as chaff. Thou shalt fan them, and the wind shall carry them away, and the whirlwind shall scatter them: and thou shalt rejoice in the LORD, and shalt glory in the Holy One of Israel” [14-16].

41.9.1.en: This is the work of God the Savior in our lives, for He transforms us from a despised worm living in the mire of this world, trodden as under foot, to raise from us a threshing instrument with sharp teeth able to thresh the mountains and crush them, or like a winnowing fork that separates the wheat from the straw... Thus God wants to befriend the despised worm in order to make it an instrument of discernment and of separating the useful wheat from the worthless straw.

41.9.2.en: God called His people “the worm Jacob,” for it lives in the clay, despised, without strength or beauty or glory, trodden by feet without care or concern. Pharaoh trod upon the people as upon a worm, but Pharaoh died, while the people enjoyed the promises of God and His salvation. Sennacherib and Nebuchadnezzar also trod upon this worm, and the whole kingdom of Assyria came to an end, and Babylon also collapsed with its mighty kings, and the worm remained alive and glorious. Thus mighty men arose through the ages such as Nero and Diocletian, and also heretics such as Arius and Nestorius... and all died and the worm remained alive, growing and being glorified. The secret of its life is that the Word of God, who became flesh, also became a worm for our sake, as the psalmist says, “But I am a worm, and no man” (Ps 22:6), that is, He condescends to become a despised man until He was counted as a worm, and so lifts us by His humility to His glory.

41.9.3.en: * “But I am a worm, and no man” (Ps 22:6).

41.9.4.en: But I speak now not in the person of Adam, but I speak originally of Myself, I, Jesus Christ. I was born without the seed of man according to the flesh, so that I, as man, might be behind every man, that human pride might imitate My humility. “A reproach of men, and despised of the people” (Ps 22:6). By humility I became a reproach among men, so that it is said mockingly, “Thou art his disciple” (Jn 9:28), and the people despise Me.

41.9.5.en: St. Augustine By our clinging to the Lord He transforms us from a weak worm, incapable of work, into a threshing instrument able to crush the mountains, which represent the works of the old man, that he may enjoy the blessings of the new life.

41.9.6.en: If our old man has become like mountains by his hard evil works, and like hills that no one can move, it is God alone who touches the mountains and they smoke (Ps 104:32). He makes us, in Christ Jesus our Lord, a new sharp threshing instrument, to thresh the mountains and crush them and fan the hills like chaff, without age touching us, and we do not lose our strength or have our abilities weaken with time. This is what delights our souls in the Lord, the Renewer of our life, and we glory in the new Holy One of Israel.

41.10.0.en: 17 “When the poor and needy seek water, and there is none, and their tongue faileth for thirst, I the LORD will hear them, I the God of Israel will not forsake them. 18 I will open rivers in high places, and fountains in the midst of the valleys: I will make the wilderness a pool of water, and the dry land springs of water. 19 I will plant in the wilderness the cedar, the shittah tree, and the myrtle, and the oil tree; I will set in the desert the cypress, and the oak, and the box tree together: 20 That they may see, and know, and consider, and understand together, that the hand of the LORD hath done this, and the Holy One of Israel hath created it.”

41.10.1.en: As the prophet Isaiah looks to the Messianic age as the age of the waters of the Holy Spirit, he sees the wilderness turned into an oasis overflowing with water, changed from a desert into a fruitful divine garden.

41.10.2.en: This figure is repeated several times (Isa 35:1-10; 43:18-21; 49:9-11; 48:21; 55:13).

41.11.0.en: In former times God brought water out of the rock for His thirsty people (Ex 17:1-7; Num 20:1-13; Isa 48:21). And in the second Exodus He does what is greater: He causes rivers to burst forth on the high barren heights and springs in the valleys; for the Lord Christ gives a new water that changes the face of the earth, turning the desert of our hearts into His spiritual Paradise, and our inner wilderness into a divine oasis, so that spiritual trees grow in us that bear delicious spiritual fruit: “I will plant in the wilderness the cedar, the shittah tree, and the myrtle, and the oil tree...” [19].

41.12.0.en: How beautiful is the phrase: “That they may see, and know, and consider, and understand together, that the hand of the LORD hath done this, and the Holy One of Israel hath created it” [20]... We behold the work of the Lord in us, and we come to know its secrets, and we contemplate the surpassing things and understand what cannot be grasped, because all this is from the hand of the holy Savior and from His creation.

41.12.1.en: St. John Chrysostom speaks in the person of the Savior, saying:

41.12.2.en: [Who can equal Me in generosity? I am Father and brother and bridegroom and home and food and clothing and root of all that you desire; I will not leave you in need of anything.

41.12.3.en: I will also be a servant to you, for I came not to be ministered unto, but to minister.

41.12.4.en: I am also friend and member and head and brother and sister and mother; I am everything, only be a friend to Me!

41.12.5.en: For your sake I became poor, and for your sake I was a beggar.

41.12.6.en: For your sake I prayed, and for your sake I was buried.

41.12.7.en: In heaven I ask the Father about you.

41.12.8.en: You are everything to Me: brother and co-heir and friend and member.

41.12.9.en: What more do you want than this?

41.12.10.en: Why do you turn away from the One who loves you, and toil for the world?]

41.13.0.en: 21 “Produce your cause, saith the LORD; bring forth your strong reasons, saith the King of Jacob. 22 Let them bring them forth, and shew us what shall happen: let them shew the former things, what they be, that we may consider them, and know the latter end of them; or declare us things for to come. 23 Shew the things that are to come hereafter, that we may know that ye are gods: yea, do good, or do evil, that we may look and behold it together. 24 Behold, ye are of nothing, and your work of nought: an abomination is he that chooseth you. 25 I have raised him up from the north, and he is come: from the rising of the sun shall he call upon my name: and he shall come upon rulers as upon mortar, and as the potter treadeth clay. 26 Who hath declared from the beginning, that we may know? and beforetime, that we may say, He is righteous? yea, there is none that sheweth, yea, there is none that declareth, yea, there is none that heareth your words. 27 I first said to Zion, Behold, behold them: and to Jerusalem I gave one that bringeth good tidings. 28 For I beheld, and there was no man; even among them, and there was no counsellor, that, when I asked of them, could answer a word. 29 Behold, they are all vanity; their works are nothing: their molten images are wind and confusion.”

41.13.1.en: In order that the Lord may give reassurance to His people and give them trust in Him, He affirms to them that the whole future is in His hands, apart from all the gods of the nations. He asked them to ask the idols whether they are able to tell of future matters, with the aim of prophesying concerning the rise of Cyrus, since that was unexpected.

41.14.0.en: God declares of Himself that He is the first to bring good tidings to His people of the rise of Cyrus [27].

41.14.1.en: Cyrus, on his father’s side, was a Mede, and on his mother’s side a Persian, and his army included men from Media who came from the north [25] and men from Persia who came from the east [25]. The Lord Christ also came from Nazareth in the north, and He is the Sun of righteousness rising from the east.

41.14.2.en: Cyrus knew God (Ezra 1) and respected all religions, including the worship of the living God; therefore it is said: “From the rising of the sun shall he call upon my name” [25]. Perhaps he also called upon the name of the Lord Christ as being a type of Him, accomplishing salvation for the whole world. Cyrus was likened to the sheep who tread the clay, an allusion to the Lord Christ as Judge to whom all nations submit like clay in the hands of the potter... (Cyrus came upon the rulers of Babylon as upon mortar) [25].
